GCTS research notebook · 6 November 2026

Join proof rectangles with long-range markings

The 72-line Hilbert proof used about 459 million local tape steps and 4,844 symbol comparisons on its copy markings. The connected rectangle took about 44.7 billion tape steps. The same local Wang palette now checks eight proof diagrams, including the 149-line betweenness proof.

Make the links part of the checking rule

The system adds one long-range marking rule to the local Wang squares. A marking states that two specified sequences of symbols, with the same length and spacing, are equal. It includes the terminating delimiter, so the entire clause is copied. The checker verifies the endpoints against the allowed source and output ports, and then compares every symbol.

Anchor a sourceThe independent formula translator checks the fixed source plate against the hypotheses and the denied conclusion.
Check an inferenceA grounding rectangle checks an instance of one copied source schema. A resolution rectangle checks two copied parents, their pivot, and the conclusion.
Follow the dependenciesEvery parent port comes from an earlier verified output. The diagram ends with the empty clause.

Induction over the proof lines establishes that every output follows from the anchored sources. The empty final output then refutes the denied conclusion. Any finite proof word in the earlier grammar can be cut into these grounding and resolution rectangles, with a copy link for each source or parent input. The construction preserves its finite proof dependencies. The original formulas and proof records are the ones found by earlier searches. This experiment measures verification with the proposed marking rule.

Each rectangle ends at the verifier’s fixed checkpoint after its local records have been checked. Its lower boundary is pinned to that configuration. The long-range markings are part of the validity conditions for the complete diagram. The connected-rectangle comparison

The native checker and global symbol encoding are shared with the connected experiment. The marked diagram places source and parent clauses at each local rectangle’s boundary. The table gives the sum of local tape steps, before any reuse, and the additional symbol-equality work.

For Hilbert incidence, the connected tape used 97.5 times the local tape steps. The diagram also checked 4,844 symbol equalities. The two entries marked open are connected runs that reached their limits. The marked diagrams checked all eight proofs or induction obligations.

A control changed a local assumption and its local proof consistently. The local Wang rectangle still verified, while the copy marking failed against the anchored source. The checker also rejected a missing marking, an endpoint shifted by one cell, and a self-dependent line.

Check a certificate against its statement

The standalone command takes a source statement and a diagram certificate, then replays the local rectangles and checks their markings.

python3 -I -S -B source/copy_verify_v1.py \
  input/hilbert-incidence-v1.json \
  data/hilbert-copy-certificate-v1.json.gz

The archive includes all eight diagrams, source statements, searched proof records, the copy rule and the independent checker. Download the replay archive
